title: Leaders Who Speak for Us
text:
In 2011 the social psychologists Alex Haslam, Stephen Reicher and Michael Platow pulled together two decades of their own and others' research into a book that challenged the idea of leadership as a set of personal traits. They argued that leadership is a relationship between leaders and followers inside a shared group.

Drawing on experiments, field studies and historical cases, they proposed that people follow leaders whom they see as "one of us," who embody what the group stands for. Leaders also gain influence when they are seen to act for the group rather than for themselves or for outsiders, when they help define what the group is and what it values, and when they turn that shared identity into concrete structures and achievements.

In experiments by Platow and colleagues, for example, leaders who acted in a way that served the group's interests were endorsed more strongly than leaders who seemed to serve themselves or another group, even when the second leaders behaved in otherwise similar ways. The authors argued that much of the charisma people attribute to great leaders reflects how well they represent and champion their group.
lesson: People follow leaders who stand for something they share. Lead by representing and building the group's identity, not by standing above it.
people: S. Alexander Haslam, Stephen Reicher, Michael Platow
source: Haslam, S. A., Reicher, S. D., and Platow, M. J. (2011). The New Psychology of Leadership: Identity, Influence and Power. Psychology Press.
caveat: It is a theoretical synthesis rather than a single study; the evidence comes from many smaller experiments and case analyses.
